place.en: Under the cliff · the valley floor

setup.zh: 你滚下了崖，摔进一片厚苔藓里。崖壁高得看不到顶，天快黑了。
setup.en: You tumbled down the cliff into a bed of thick moss. The cliff rises out of sight; night is coming.

recap.zh: 你摔进崖下的山谷，没有哭：先查伤，再找路，活到爹来的时候。
recap.en: You fell into the valley under the cliff and did not cry: check the hurts, find the way, live till Father comes.

en: The cliff climbs out of sight into the rain.
A bed of thick, soaked moss.
When you fall, don't hurry to get up.

story.zh:
你滚了下去。

泥、石头、断枝、雨水，天和地在你眼前翻了不知多少个个儿。你本能地护住了头，后背撞上什么硬东西，疼得眼前一黑；你伸手乱抓，抓住了一根藤，藤绷得笔直，把你往下的势头拽住了一瞬——然后断了。

最后一下，你摔进了一片软的东西里。是苔藓。很厚，很软，像一床湿透了的棉被。

你躺着，没有动。你爹说过：摔了，先别急着起来，一样一样地查。
story.en:
You tumble down.

Mud, stones, broken branches, rain — sky and earth turn over before your eyes more times than you can count. You cover your head without thinking; your back strikes something hard and the world goes black with pain; you claw at anything, catch a vine, and the vine snaps taut and holds your fall for an instant — then breaks.

The last blow lands you in something soft. Moss. Very thick, very soft, like a quilt soaked through.

You lie there and do not move. Your father always said: when you fall, don't hurry to get up. Check yourself, one thing at a time.

label.en: Check yourself, one thing at a time

exits.means: checks the injuries, gets up carefully, looks for shelter and a way

story.zh:
手指，能动。脚趾，能动。膝盖破了，手掌磨掉了一层皮，后背火辣辣地疼，左手腕肿了——但骨头没断。

你这才坐起来，往上看。崖壁高得看不到顶，消失在雨雾里。

你没有喊。你在心里数：你爹被你拽进了山壁里，他没掉下来。他膝盖不好，这么大的雨，他下不来，也不该下来。他会等雨停，会顺着记号回村叫人。

所以你要做的，是活到那个时候。

你十二岁，一个人，在一个你从来没来过的山谷里，天快黑了。你没有哭。你爹说过，打猎的人在山里迷了路，头一件事是找个地方躲雨，第二件事是生火，第三件事才是害怕。

你决定，第三件事，先不做了。

雨小了些。你扶着崖壁往前走，每走一段，就在崖壁上划一道——你得记得回来的路。

这山谷很怪。外面的山都是松树、柏树、野栗子，这里却长着你从来没见过的树——叶子是银白色的，薄得透光，雨水落上去，不往下淌，而是滚成一颗一颗的珠子，挂在叶尖上，亮晶晶的，像是满树都结了露水做的果子。

地上的草也不一样。每一步踩下去，草叶都会微微发亮，一圈淡淡的光从你脚下漾开，又慢慢暗下去。

你走得很轻。不知道为什么，你觉得这里的东西都在睡觉，不该吵醒它们。

然后你看见了光。

山谷深处，一片被雨水砸出来的浅坑里，有一点银光。一明，一暗，一明，一暗——像是有什么东西在很慢很慢地呼吸。
story.en:
Fingers: they move. Toes: they move. Knees skinned, a layer of skin gone from your palms, your back burning, your left wrist swollen — but no bones broken.

Only then do you sit up and look up. The cliff rises out of sight, lost in the rain and mist.

You don't shout. You count it out in your head: you hauled your father against the rock; he didn't fall. With his knee, in rain like this, he can't climb down, and he shouldn't. He will wait for the rain to stop and follow the marks back to the village for help.

So what you have to do is stay alive until then.

You are twelve, alone, in a valley you have never seen, and night is coming. You don't cry. Your father always said: a hunter lost in the mountains first finds shelter from the rain, second makes a fire, and only third gets frightened.

You decide to leave the third thing for now.

The rain eases. You feel your way along the cliff, and every little way you scratch a line on the rock — you have to remember the way back.

It is a strange valley. The mountains outside are pine and cypress and wild chestnut; here grow trees you have never seen — silver-white leaves, so thin the light shows through. The rain does not run off them; it beads into drops that hang at every leaf tip, glittering, as if the trees were heavy with fruit made of dew.

The grass is different too. At every step the blades glow faintly, and a pale ring of light spreads from your foot and slowly fades.

You walk very softly. You don't know why, but everything here seems to be asleep, and you should not wake it.

Then you see the light.

Deep in the valley, in a shallow pit the rain has beaten out, there is a point of silver. Bright, dim, bright, dim — as if something were breathing, very, very slowly.
